summary: Specifies a framework for policy-based control over admission control decisions, describing the roles and interactions of the components involved. This is an informational memo.

plainLanguage.summary: RFC 2753 describes how a network can check whether a resource reservation follows its rules as well as whether capacity is available. A router asks a policy decision service for an answer and then applies it, but this memo does not define the policy rules or the communication protocol.

subtitle: A framework for deciding whether network resource requests meet administrative policies.

tldr.problem: Reservation protocols can check resource requests against available capacity, but network managers may also need decisions based on identity, credentials, agreements, or time.
tldr.mechanism: A Policy Enforcement Point on a network node sends a request to a Policy Decision Point, which returns the decision the enforcement point applies. An optional local point can make an initial decision.
tldr.outcome: RFC 2753 is an Informational framework. It describes roles, requirements, and example policy situations, but does not define a particular policy or PEP-to-PDP protocol.

today: RFC 2753 is an Informational framework published in January 2000. It does not specify an Internet standard or a particular policy-control protocol.

sections.title: Why Admission Control Needs Policy
sections.content:
Integrated Services and RSVP let an application request a particular quality of service (QoS), such as reserved bandwidth. In the model described here, admission control compares the request with available capacity. It does not by itself let a provider decide based on who made the request, what application made it, or when it arrived.

RFC 2753 sets out a framework for adding policy-based decisions to admission control. RSVP is its main example, but the framework is intended to apply to other QoS settings as well. It describes the pieces needed to enforce policies rather than prescribing a specific set of policies.
sections.plainLanguage: A network may have enough capacity for a request and still need to check whether its rules allow it. This framework adds that policy check to a resource reservation decision.

sections.title: What the Framework Requires
sections.content:
The memo says the framework should support preemption, which removes an existing reservation to make room for another. It also calls for monitoring and accounting information, recovery from failures and network partitions, and operation when some network nodes do not implement policy control.

The framework is meant to support different policies, including provider agreements and relative priorities. It must scale at least as well as RSVP, including for large multicast flows. The policy architecture should also limit theft and denial-of-service risks and let decision points verify one another's identities.
sections.plainLanguage: The design must support more than accepting or rejecting a request. It needs to account for use, recover from failures, work across different providers, and operate when some routers do not make policy decisions.

sections.title: The PEP, PDP and Optional LPDP
sections.content:
The Policy Enforcement Point (PEP) runs on a network node and applies policy decisions. The Policy Decision Point (PDP) makes the final decision and may be a separate policy server. A node may also have a Local Policy Decision Point (LPDP) for local checks, or the PDP may be on the same node as the PEP.

The PEP builds a request from the triggering event and available policy information. If an LPDP is present, it can return a partial result. The PEP then sends the request and policy elements to the PDP, which returns the final decision. The PEP must enforce that decision. The PEP must contact the PDP even when the original request contains no policy objects, so omitting those objects cannot bypass the policy check.
sections.plainLanguage: The PEP is the part of a router that applies the answer. The PDP makes the final decision, even if a local policy point checked the request first.

sections.title: Policy Situations the Framework Covers
sections.content:
The examples include rules based on time of day, user identity, or credentials. Providers may have bilateral agreements about access and accounting; boundary nodes can add policy information to a reservation request and rewrite it as the request crosses administrative domains.

Priority rules can allow a higher-priority reservation to preempt a lower-priority one. The memo also discusses prepaid tokens whose remaining service value is reduced as requests are accepted, and sender-specified limits on which receivers may reserve resources. These are examples and open design questions, not policies defined by the framework.
sections.plainLanguage: Examples include time-based access, provider agreements, priority reservations, prepaid service, and limits on who may join a multicast reservation. The memo explains the situations without choosing the rules for them.

sections.title: Communication and Security
sections.content:
When the PDP is outside the network node, the PEP and PDP need a communication protocol. The memo says it should be reliable, add little delay, carry variable-length opaque objects, support PEP-initiated request-and-response exchanges, and allow asynchronous notices in both directions. It does not select or specify that protocol.

The memo recommends protecting the channel between policy clients and servers with IPsec, using both the Authentication Header and Encapsulating Security Payload to provide confidentiality, origin authentication, integrity, and replay prevention. For RSVP signaling, it also identifies RSVP MD5 authentication as a possible protection between network elements.
sections.plainLanguage: The PEP and PDP need a quick, reliable way to exchange requests and decisions. The memo recommends protecting this channel with IPsec, but leaves the actual PEP-to-PDP protocol unspecified.
